title: B1 Writing Quiz 6 — Sports, Hobbies & Free Time

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had more free time, I would learn to paint.
If I have more free time, I would learn to paint.
If I had more free time, I will learn to paint.
If I would have more free time, I would learn to paint.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I had more free time, I would learn to paint.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If he had trained harder, he wouldn't lose the match.
If he had trained harder, he wouldn't have lost the match.
If he trained harder, he wouldn't have lost the match.
If he would have trained harder, he wouldn't have lost the match.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If he had trained..., he wouldn't have lost...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This tournament is watched by millions of fans.
This tournament watches by millions of fans.
This tournament is watching by millions of fans.
This tournament watch by millions of fans.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is watched by millions of fans.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The match was postponed due to rain.
The match postponed due to rain.
The match was postpone due to rain.
The match is postponed due to rain.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was postponed due to rain.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The coach who trained the team retired last year.
The coach which trained the team retired last year.
The coach whom trained the team retired last year.
The coach, who trained the team, retired last year but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The coach who trained the team...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My local gym, which opened last year, is always busy.
My local gym which opened last year is always busy but.
My local gym, that opened last year, is always busy.
My local gym which opened last year, is always busy.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'My local gym, which opened last year, is always busy.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That score can't be right, let me check again.
That score can't to be right, let me check again.
That score can't being right, let me check again.
That score cann't be right, let me check again.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' + base verb expresses a confident negative deduction: 'that score can't be right.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The team could be practicing right now.
The team could being practicing right now.
The team could to be practicing right now.
The team coulds be practicing right now.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the team could be practicing.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've played five matches this season.
I've been playing five matches this season.
I've play five matches this season.
I'm playing five matches this season already.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've played five matches.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been practicing the guitar for three years.
I've practiced the guitar since three years.
I'm practicing the guitar for three years already.
I've been practice the guitar for three years.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been practicing... for three years.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have joined a new club.")
options: He said that he has joined a new club.
He said that he had joined a new club.
He said that he joined a new club already.
He said he have joined a new club.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'he had joined a new club.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "Which team do you support?")
options: He asked me which team do I support.
He asked me which team I supported.
He asked me which team did I support.
He asked me which team I support.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'he asked me which team I supported.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to play football every weekend as a child.
I use to play football every weekend as a child.
I was used to play football every weekend as a child.
I used to playing football every weekend as a child.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to play football every weekend.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm used to training early in the morning now.
I'm used to train early in the morning now.
I use to training early in the morning now.
I'm used training to early in the morning now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to training early in the morning.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She decided to take up swimming last summer.
She decided to take swimming up to last summer.
She decided to take up to swimming last summer.
She decided to take swimming last summer up.
questions.explanation: 'Take up' means 'start a new hobby': 'take up swimming.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Athletes always warm up before a race.
Athletes always warm the race up before.
Athletes always warm up to before a race.
Athletes always warm before a race up.
questions.explanation: 'Warm up' means 'prepare the body before exercise': 'warm up before a race.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite the injury, she finished the race.
Despite of the injury, she finished the race.
Although the injury, she finished the race.
Despite the injury was serious, she finished the race.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the injury, she finished the race.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He missed training all week. As a result, he wasn't picked for the game.
He missed training all week, as a result he wasn't picked for the game.
As a result he missed training all week he wasn't picked for the game.
He missed training all week as a result, he wasn't picked for the game.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'He missed training all week. As a result, he wasn't picked for the game.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have enough players for a full team.
We don't have players enough for a full team.
We don't have enough of players for a full team.
We hasn't enough players for a full team.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough players.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My brother is really keen on cycling.
My brother is really keen for cycling.
My brother is really keen at cycling.
My brother is really keen to cycling.
questions.explanation: 'Keen on' + noun/gerund means 'enthusiastic about': 'keen on cycling.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a sports club you haven't met, asking to join?
options: Hey there,
Dear Sir or Madam,
Yo,
Hiya,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir or Madam,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a named club coordinator?
options: Yours faithfully,
Best regards,
Later,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Best regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could send me the training schedule.
I was wondering if you could to send me the training schedule.
I was wondering could you sending me the training schedule.
I wonder if you send could me the training schedule.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could send me the schedule.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the athlete.' and 'The athlete's record still stands.'?
options: This is the athlete whose record still stands.
This is the athlete who record still stands.
This is the athlete which record still stands.
This is the athlete's record who still stands.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the athlete whose record still stands.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never played such a difficult opponent before.
I have played never such a difficult opponent before.
Never I have played such a difficult opponent before.
I have played such a difficult opponent never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never played such an opponent.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the final has been rescheduled.
I'd like to know whether has the final been rescheduled?
I'd like to know, whether the final has been rescheduled.
I'd like to know whether the final has been rescheduled?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time tomorrow, I ___ in the marathon.
options: will run
will be running
am running
run
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be running'.

questions.question: By the end of the season, the team ___ twenty matches.
options: will play
will have played
plays
is playing
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have played'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly, stretch your muscles. Secondly, warm up slowly. Finally, start the workout.
Firstly we stretch muscles secondly warm finally workout.
Finally stretch the muscles, firstly warm, secondly start workout.
Secondly firstly stretch muscles, finally warm up.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't miss the final match, would you?
You wouldn't miss the final match, do you?
You wouldn't miss the final match, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't miss the final match, will you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't miss..., would you?'
